transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-11-23 14:30 PST | Duration: ~42m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Carlos Rivera (Redwood) - Sarah Li, Tom Brooks, Priya Nair, Jeff Morris (Aurora)

Summary (auto): Quick Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV cache. SE showed cost model spreadsheet and sample throughput/latency graphs. Customer asked about PII, KMS, and how fallback works for cold cache.

00:00 Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you making time. quick agenda — we'll run through batching fundamentals, show how prefix and KV cache behave, then step through the cost model and a few examples from similar payments customers.
00:18 Sarah Li: thanks, Maya. quick note — our priority is predictable latency for the payments flows, plus tight data handling (PII) controls, so we'll be listening for private deployment and KMS notes.
00:28 Carlos Rivera: great, we'll flag security details when relevant. Tom, can you confirm the baseline? you had said 200 qps peak and 60k tokens/minute?
00:37 Tom Brooks: yeah that's right, peak is around 180-220 qps in US-east during batch settlement, typical request sizes are 60-400 tokens, most are short (~90 tokens).
00:49 Carlos Rivera: perfect, that distribution matters for batching heuristics. ok slide share — show of the cost model (link: drive/redwood/optimize/aurora-batch-model.xlsx)
01:05 Maya Chen: note, numbers in the sheet assume our hosted SKU pricing for OpenQuant models; we can swap in dedicated pricing for a committed pool.
01:20 Carlos Rivera: first concept: batching. there are two primary approaches we recommend: dynamic batching (request coalescing with latency-aware thresholds) and fixed micro-batches for predictable throughput. dynamic gives best cost efficiency at variable load, fixed is easier to SLO.
01:40 Sarah Li: what about tail latency? dynamic sounds like it could add jitter.
01:46 Carlos Rivera: correct — dynamic batching can increase tail latency slightly because it waits to fill a batch, but our runtime uses latency windows and max-wait knobs — e.g., you can cap wait to 20ms so 95th stays tight. also we do priority queues so high-priority payments requests can bypass batching or use smaller max-wait.
02:10 Jeff Morris: so what's the tradeoff in cost? like ballpark numbers.
02:16 Carlos Rivera: quick example from the sheet — with Aurora-like mix, moving from no-batching to dynamic batching reduced per-token infra cost by ~28% in our hosted runs; fixed micro-batch (size 4) gave ~18% savings but predictable latency. these assume a KV cache hit-rate around 35%.
02:35 Tom Brooks: how's the KV/prefix cache modeled? that 35% is optimistic for us maybe. we have lots of unique customer messages.
02:42 Carlos Rivera: good question. prefix cache is most effective when you have repeated prefixes — for e.g., templated confirmations, policy text, or reused system prompts. KV cache stores KV cache for decoder states across conversation turns which benefits long sessions. the model has parameters: hit-rate, average cached tokens per hit, and the cost of storing (memory footprint translates to an infra delta). in spreadsheet there's a tab 'kv-assumptions' where we tune those numbers.
03:10 Sarah Li: do you do any privacy-safe caching? we can't persist raw PII keys.
03:16 Maya Chen: we have options — prefix caching can be configured to scrub or hash identifiers before caching, and with Private deployment you control KMS; for hosted we support customer-managed keys (CMK) so cached KVs are encrypted and keys are under your control.
03:34 Priya Nair: if you scrub, does that reduce hit-rate?
03:38 Carlos Rivera: it depends — scrubbing normalized tokens can actually increase hit-rate because variable identifiers are removed, but you lose some specificity. it's a balance; we'll model both scrubbed and un-scrubbed hit-rates in the benchmark.
03:55 Maya Chen: next piece — cold cache penalty and warm-up. if you enable KV cache with a cold start, initial requests might see 10-30% higher latency until common prefixes populate. we recommend a short priming run or priming the cache via a replay of representative traffic before going live.
04:20 Tom Brooks: can Redwood prime cache from our historical logs?
04:24 Carlos Rivera: yes — for Dedicated/Private we can ingest a historical prompt set to pre-warm KV and prefix caches; for Hosted we support controlled replay under the pilot agreement. we'll need sanitized logs and a permit from your security team.
04:40 Jeff Morris: shown in the sheet — what's the infrastructure cost hit for large KV caches?
04:45 Carlos Rivera: it's small relative to GPU time for most workloads. e.g., storing 50M KV entries on our runtime adds a modest RAM footprint and slight increase in instance sizing, typically +5-12% infra cost, but token savings often outweigh that within weeks. numbers in the sheet show ROI curves — 4-6 weeks payback at 30% hit-rate.
05:05 Sarah Li: curious about model variants — if you fallback from a quantized variant to full-precision on cold paths, how does that add to latency?
05:12 Carlos Rivera: fallback happens per-request and adds a small penalty; we instrument fallbacks and can route cold cache requests to higher-throughput nodes or use a hybrid policy. again the cost model has a fallback tax parameter (we used 8-12% latency increase in examples).
05:30 Maya Chen: demo time — Carlos will show a quick run with three scenarios: no batching, dynamic batching, and dynamic batching + KV cache with a 40% hit-rate (demo data).
05:38 [screen share noise, faint keyboard]
05:52 Carlos Rivera: ok running synthetic workload — watch the qps and 95th ms. scenario A (no batching) 95th ~120ms, tokens/sec X. scenario B (dynamic batching) 95th ~135ms but cost down ~30%. scenario C (dynamic + KV) 95th ~110ms and cost down ~45% vs baseline. note the KV scenario has better end-to-end because it avoids re-generation for cached prefixes.
07:20 Tom Brooks: that lower tail in scenario C surprised me — I thought caching might increase variability.
07:27 Carlos Rivera: in our runs KV cache reduced compute per request so scheduler overhead drops; with well-tuned cache it can actually tighten tails if cache hit-rate is stable. but sudden cache churn can spike tails — we guard with throttles and graceful degradation to avoid cascading latency.
08:00 Priya Nair: k, security quick Q: does Redwood log raw prompts in hosted? retention and redaction?
08:07 Maya Chen: hosted logs are encrypted; retention configurable per account. we provide audit logs and optional automatic redaction. for regulated customers we recommend Private deployment or Hosted + CMK + strict retention windows. we can provide SOC2 report and our redaction docs (link: drive/redwood/security/sanitization.pdf).
08:30 Sarah Li: good. what's the pilot we should expect?
08:34 Maya Chen: typical pilot is 2-4 weeks: we first get a representative prompt set and traffic pattern, we run a benchmarking job in a dedicated sandbox, evaluate hit-rates, tune batching knobs, and deliver a final cost/latency report. we'll include recommendations: batch size, max-wait, cache scrub rules, and rough infra sizing.
09:00 Jeff Morris: do we need to commit to Dedicated for caching features?
09:05 Carlos Rivera: no — caching works on Hosted; Dedicated gives more predictable throughput and isolation. Private gives full infra control and KMS in your VPC. You can start on Hosted pilot and move to Dedicated/Private later.
09:20 Tom Brooks: can you show the spreadsheet assumptions again? the tab with token pricing and batch multiplier?
09:27 Carlos Rivera: sure — see column F-H. we model total cost = compute_cost_per_token * effective_tokens + infra_mem_surcharge. effective_tokens accounts for tokens avoided by cache hits. we also show sensitivity to hit-rate from 0-60%.
09:45 Maya Chen: a quick note on quantization — using 4-bit quantized models reduces GPU memory and can lower infra cost ~20-40% depending on model; but you should validate for quality. Redwood Optimize flags quantization-risk and suggests model family/quantization combos per workload.
10:05 Sarah Li: quality regressions are our main worry. how do you guard against regressions when changing model or quantization?
10:10 Carlos Rivera: we integrate prompt-set based evals into the rollout — Redwood Optimize can run small eval suites on new variants and alert on regressions beyond your threshold (we can set fail-on-regression). also gradual rollouts and canary traffic help detect issues.
10:30 Tom Brooks: ok practical — for our pilot, we'll provide a 48-hour sample of peak window, plus a list of 200 canonical prompts. you will run the bench and share hit-rate estimates, right?
10:38 Maya Chen: yes. Carlos will run the bench, we'll include two configs: (A) dynamic batching with 20ms max-wait, (B) dynamic + KV with scrub rules you define.
10:50 Priya Nair: and you'll include KMS notes and data retention in the deliverable?
10:55 Maya Chen: yes, security appendix included.
11:05 Jeff Morris: any gotchas we should know?
11:08 Carlos Rivera: monitor hit-rate variance — if your traffic is extremely diverse and prefixes unique per user, cache won't help much. also watch for long-tail queries that blow up token usage — set hard token limits per request and instrument token distributions.
11:30 Sarah Li: makes sense. thanks — this is helpful.
11:35 Maya Chen: recap of next steps: we'll send the cost model spreadsheet, Carlos runs benchmark, and security will exchange docs. finalize pilot kickoff next week.
11:48 Tom Brooks: we'll send the sample prompts and open a Jira/secure s3 share for logs.
11:53 Maya Chen: perfect, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with calendar invite and the pricing sheet.
12:00 [meeting ends]

Notes: occasional transcription errors in product names (e.g., "KV cache" spoken as "K-V cash"), minor speaker attribution artifacts. Links referenced: drive/redwood/optimize/aurora-batch-model.xlsx, drive/redwood/security/sanitization.pdf.
